title: Heaven on earth
hookLine: the Orthodox see the Divine Liturgy as joining heaven's worship now

cards: An old Russian chronicle tells of envoys sent by a prince of Kiev to Constantinople. They're led into the great church there while the Liturgy is being sung: chant, lamps, incense, a dome overhead.
Back home, they struggle to describe it. The chronicle gives their report, in substance: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth.
We only know that God dwells there among people, and we can't forget that beauty. You heard the envoys' story back on day eight hundred five.
Whatever historians make of it, it's a striking thing to say about a church service. It's the last stop on the Orthodox way of the heart.

teach.b: For Orthodox Christians, that line isn't only a traveler's compliment. It's close to how their church describes the Divine Liturgy itself.
Not a play about heaven, not a memory of heaven, but a joining in, now, with worship already going on there. The Bible gives them the picture.

In Revelation, John is shown the throne of God, and creatures around it who "rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come." A song with no gaps in it.
The Liturgy steps into that song for a while.

teach.h: YE ARE COME UNTO MOUNT SION.
teach.b: The letter to the Hebrews tells ordinary believers: "ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels." Ye are come. Not someday.

teach.h: A ROOM FULLER THAN IT LOOKS.
teach.b: The saints on the icons stand with the people, so the room is never only as full as it looks.
Incense goes up, and Revelation has that picture as well: the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, rising before God.
That's why yesterday's hymn asked everyone to lay their cares aside: they're about to stand in a crowded room.
Look back across this week: guarding the door of the heart, tears that wash, a knot for each prayer, an elder to help you hear, a mountain at prayer, cares set down.
It all leads here, to the plain claim the Orthodox make about their worship: heaven is not far off. It's near.

how: Orthodox Christians gather for the Divine Liturgy on Sundays and feasts; with icons, incense and chant, the service is understood as a sharing in the worship of heaven, and it leads to communion.

o: a church so grand it looks like a palace
worship that joins heaven's song here and now
a calm, happy feeling after a very good day

it says ye are come: already.

games.q: you're one of the envoys, home from Constantinople. the prince asks what the Liturgy in the great church was like. what do you say?
o: it was long, and we couldn't follow the language.
we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth.
it was much like any other service.
games.why: the chronicle gives their answer: they didn't know whether they were in heaven or on earth, and couldn't forget that beauty.

practice: Let the room around you grow larger in your mind: not empty, but full. If you pray, say the line from Revelation, holy, holy, holy, and let it join a song the text says never stops.
If you don't, simply sit as if you were in very good company, unhurried, unseen, and not alone.

wordCard.voice: Heaven on earth. The Orthodox picture of the Divine Liturgy: not watching heaven from far away, but joining its worship now.

orig.note: Greek: the Divine Liturgy, the Orthodox name for the service of communion.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven is near. Tomorrow, a new room in the house: Francis of Assisi.

sources.ref: The Russian Primary Chronicle (the envoys of Prince Vladimir at Constantinople)
